newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage-backed players eye U.S. Treasury auctions.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage-backed players eye U.S. Treasury auctions.

text.p: Mortgage-backed securities prices were lower but spreads to U.S. Treasuries remained tight.

Market participants said activity this session was subdued with market participants keeping an eye on the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly refunding. The Treasury's three-year note auction produced yields of 6.041 percent.
Market participants said that investors will be closely watching the Treasury's $12 billion 10-year note sale Wednesday and its $10 billion sale of 30-year bonds on Thursday.
"There was some activity in the morning, but nothing special. There were no big surprises in the 3-year auction ... the bid-to-cover was about average," said one market player.
The bid-to-cover ratio is the number of bids received in a Treasury securities auction compared to the number of bids accepted.
In addition to paying close attention to the refunding process, mortgage investors continue to digest the July employment report released last week and the sharp decline in prices seen last Friday.

"There are a lot of people still reeling from Friday's employment report. They are trying to understand the data and the decline in Treasury prices," said William Gooch, vice president at Legg Mason Wood Walker. He added that investors who were concerned about prepayments prior to the report may now be reconsidering a move out of mortgages or down-in-coupon.
"If the auction is well received it will give the market a sense of optimism. If it is well received, yields should decline. Spreads on MBS could possible widen," said Gooch.

Meantime, one market participant noted that there was talk in the market of a large buyer of Federal National Mortgage Association 8.0 percent coupons. She too agreed that there would be more of wait and see approach among investors. "Most have done what they wanted to do -- extend or shorten duration. So people will be waiting for the next couple of weeks" to see more economic data, the market observer said.
